analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and enforcement when employers retaliate against workers trying to organize or bargain.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and died there when the 115th Congress ended, despite 115 Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The WAGE Act would have rewritten the main federal labor law to give real teeth to workers' rights to organize and bargain. It would have let the National Labor Relations Board impose civil fines of up to $50,000 per violation (up to $100,000 for repeat offenders), doubled the back pay owed to illegally fired workers, let workers sue employers directly in court, made NLRB orders enforceable immediately instead of waiting years for court approval, and required employers to bargain once a union wins a representation vote. It also narrowed the 'supervisor' and 'independent contractor' loopholes so more workers are covered.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who try to organize, join a union, or discuss pay with co-workers, and would-be union members whose employers currently delay or stall first contracts. Unionized workers earn roughly 25% more than comparable non-union workers, according to the bill's own findings.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the NLRB to award back pay plus liquidated damages equal to twice the back pay, with no reduction for interim earnings, to workers whose employers fire them or cause serious economic harm by breaking labor law.

Creates civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation — doubled to $100,000 for employers with recent violations — for firing or seriously harming workers for exercising NLRA rights, with potential personal liability for directors and officers.
Gives workers a private right of action to sue employers in federal court for certain violations within 180 days, instead of relying solely on the NLRB to prosecute their case.

Requires the NLRB to order an employer to bargain when a majority of votes in an election favor union representation, and lets the Board order bargaining when employer interference taints an election — instead of rerunning elections indefinitely.

Makes NLRB orders self-enforcing upon issuance, with fines up to $10,000 per day of noncompliance, eliminating the current requirement that the Board petition a court of appeals for enforcement, which has caused long delays.
Expands coverage by tightening the 'supervisor' definition and applying a stricter test against misclassifying employees as independent contractors, so more workers are protected by the law.

Speeds up first contracts by mandating a bargaining timetable — negotiation, then federal mediation, then binding arbitration — since workers and employers fail to reach an initial agreement in as many as half of new organizing campaigns.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — including large service, retail, and manufacturing employers, staffing firms, and gig-economy platforms — would face civil fines, doubled back-pay awards, personal liability for executives, immediate enforcement of NLRB orders, and joint liability for workers supplied by staffing agencies. Unionized or newly organized workplaces would also share gains with workers through bargaining.

drawbacks.text: The civil penalties and doubled damages apply to employers of any size, though the Board must consider employer size when setting fines, so small businesses with compliance mistakes could face significant costs.

The binding arbitration mechanism for first contracts — after 90 days of bargaining and 30 days of mediation, an arbitration panel sets terms binding for two years — replaces negotiated terms with arbitrator-imposed ones that neither side may have chosen.

The Board's orders would become self-enforcing and effective immediately, subject to court review later — a major shift in power from courts to the NLRB that critics view as reducing employer due process.
Narrowing the independent-contractor exemption would sweep many freelancers and gig workers into the labor law's coverage, changing how millions of people are classified at work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill fixes real, documented problems: current law has no civil penalties, no private lawsuits, and NLRB orders require a separate court petition to enforce, all of which employers can outlast. The costs fall almost entirely on employers who violate the law, though the binding-arbitration shortcut for first contracts and tighter contractor classification raise legitimate concerns about imposed terms and classification for independent workers. On balance the bill was designed to be a strong deterrent, and the main honest objection is not that workers wouldn't benefit but that employers would bear concentrated, sometimes executive-level, liability.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a markup or sent it anywhere, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott introduced the WAGE Act on December 5, 2017, with 32 original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
That referral was the only action ever taken; the bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a hearing in the record, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
The bill attracted 115 cosponsors, all Democrats and none Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced civil penalties, doubled back-pay awards, direct lawsuits, and immediate NLRB enforcement are better off because the bill died in committee, since the law's remedies for firing union supporters remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced new penalties

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — 115 Democratic cosponsors and zero Republicans — and the Republican House majority never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Large service, retail, and manufacturing employers
industries.note: These employers would face civil fines up to $100,000 per violation, doubled back-pay awards, direct worker lawsuits, and immediate enforcement of NLRB orders — costs they avoid under current law because NLRA remedies carry no civil penalties and are hard to enforce. Their gain from the bill's death is the absence of these penalties.

The bill's stricter independent-contractor test would classify many gig workers as employees covered by the labor law, and joint-and-several liability would make platform and staffing companies responsible for violations involving workers supplied by others.

Bargaining orders upon winning an election, faster binding first contracts, and stronger remedies against retaliation would make organizing more likely to succeed, expanding union membership and dues and raising covered workers' pay.
